story: When NASA launched the James Webb Space Telescope in December 2021, engineers faced a terrifying reality. Bound for a halo orbit nearly one million miles from Earth, the observatory had to unfold itself in deep space without any hope of a crewed repair mission. The entire multi-billion-dollar observatory relied on 344 potential single-point failures. If just one of these mechanisms failed—from the release of the five-layer sunshield to the latching of the gold-plated beryllium mirror segments—the mission would be crippled. To make matters worse, the launch had to be precisely calculated because the spacecraft could not use its thrusters to slow down upon arrival, as firing them forward would risk baking its ultra-sensitive infrared instruments in the unshielded heat of the Sun. Despite these harrowing odds, every single deployment step executed successfully, opening a brand-new infrared window to the universe.
angle: The James Webb Space Telescope had 344 potential single-point failures that all had to work perfectly nearly a million miles from Earth, with zero chance of a repair crew.

claims.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021.
JWST launched on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana.
The telescope operates near the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, about 1.5 million kilometers or 930,000 miles from Earth.
The launch and deployment of JWST featured 344 potential single-point failures.
The spacecraft cannot use its thrusters to slow down when arriving at L2 because the sunshield must remain between the telescope and the Sun.
NASA led the design and development in partnership with the European Space Agency and Canadian Space Agency.
